title: CRYPTOGRAPHY
body:
The course where [[ABSTRACT ALGEBRA]] stops being abstract. MATH 2101 is its stated prerequisite
and it is the cleanest chain in the degree: 2101 spends a term building [[Group]]s, [[Ring]]s, and
[[Finite Field]]s, and 4111 spends a term using them, mostly without adding new mathematics.
[[RSA]] is [[Modular Arithmetic]] plus [[Lagrange's Theorem]] plus the extended
[[Euclidean Algorithm]]; [[AES]] is arithmetic in $GF(2^8)$; [[Diffie-Hellman]] is exponentiation
in a [[Cyclic Group]]; [[Elliptic Curve Cryptography]] is the same protocol with the group swapped
out. The course runs forwards in history, from ciphers you break with a pencil and a letter-count
to the ones the internet currently runs on, and the argument it makes along the way is that
**every one of them was broken by a statistical or algebraic structure its designers did not think
mattered**.

Two habits it is really teaching. First, **Kerckhoffs's principle**: the algorithm is public and
only the key is secret, so a scheme that needs obscurity is not a scheme. Second, **state your
adversary**: "secure" is meaningless without a named attack model, and the discipline is to assume
the strongest one because the assumption is free and the mistake is not.

## Topics

### Classical cryptography and cryptanalysis

The pencil-and-paper era, kept because every modern failure is one of these failures wearing better
clothes.

- [[Classical Ciphers]] is the block's hub: shift, affine, general substitution, and Vigenère, all
  of them arithmetic in $\mathbb{Z}_{26}$. The affine cipher's $\gcd(a,26)=1$ condition is the
  invertibility theorem from [[Modular Arithmetic]] turning up in week one.
- [[Transposition Cipher]] is the other half: permute the positions instead of replacing the
  characters. Both senses of [[Permutation]] are in play at once, the count from
  [[DISCRETE MATH]] and the structure from [[Permutation Group]].
- [[Cryptanalysis]] is the block's real content: frequency analysis, the index of coincidence,
  Kasiski, and the attack-model ladder from ciphertext-only up to chosen-ciphertext. It is where
  the course establishes that a $26!$ key space is worth nothing.

### Symmetric key cryptography

One shared key, and the fastest thing available. This is what actually encrypts your data.

- [[Symmetric Key Cryptography]] is the hub: the key distribution problem, the stream/block split,
  and Shannon's confusion and diffusion, which every design below is an attempt to buy cheaply.
- [[Stream Cipher]] XORs the message with a generated keystream. The one-time pad is the ideal, the
  LFSR is the classic generator, and the note lands directly on [[Shift Register]] and
  [[Boolean Algebra]] from [[COMPUTING MACHINERY 2]].
- [[Feistel Network]] is the construction that makes any function invertible, and therefore DES:
  S-boxes, P-boxes, and the reason decryption is the same circuit run with the subkeys reversed.
- [[AES]] is where the algebra becomes explicit. The state is a matrix of bytes, the S-box is
  inversion in $GF(2^8)$, and MixColumn is [[LINEAR ALGEBRA]] with the scalars in a
  [[Finite Field]].
- [[Modes of Operation]] is how you encrypt more than one block, and where most real bugs live.
  ECB leaks structure, CBC chains, CTR turns the block cipher into a stream cipher, and none of
  them detects tampering.

### Public key cryptography

Two keys, and the answer to the problem symmetric cryptography cannot touch.

- [[Public Key Cryptography]] is the hub: trapdoor one-way functions, why the security is an
  *assumption* rather than a theorem, and why every deployment is hybrid.
- [[RSA]] is the first practical scheme and the one built entirely out of notes that already
  exist. Euler's totient, modular inversion, and a correctness proof that is one line of
  [[Lagrange's Theorem]].
- [[Discrete Logarithm Problem]] is the other hardness assumption, and the note that pins down what
  "hard" has to mean: average case, not worst case, which is why [[NP-Complete]] is the wrong tool.
- [[Diffie-Hellman]] agrees a shared secret over an open channel, and has no authentication
  whatsoever, which is the standing lesson about what mathematics cannot fix.
- [[ElGamal]] turns that exchange into an encryption scheme, randomised for free and fatally
  sensitive to nonce reuse.

### Hash functions and message integrity

- [[Cryptographic Hash Function]] carries the three resistances, Merkle-Damgård and the sponge, and
  **the distinction from [[Hashing]] in [[INFORMATION STRUCTURES]]**, which is the same word for an
  almost opposite design brief.
- [[HMAC]] adds a key, which is what turns integrity into authenticity. It exists in the shape it
  does because the obvious construction falls to length extension.

### Digital signatures

- [[Digital Signature]] reverses the key roles: sign with the private key, verify with the public
  one. RSA-PSS and DSA, non-repudiation as the property a MAC cannot give, and existential
  unforgeability under chosen-message attack as the security definition. **A hash collision is a
  forgery**, which is why SHA-1's break retired it everywhere.

### Advanced and emerging

- [[Elliptic Curve Cryptography]] keeps every protocol and changes the group. The points on a curve
  over a finite field form an abelian group, index calculus does not apply to it, and that missing
  attack is the entire reason a 256-bit key replaces a 3072-bit one.
- [[Post-Quantum Cryptography]] is the deadline. Shor kills every public-key scheme above; Grover
  only halves symmetric key lengths. Lattices, hash-based signatures, and code-based schemes are
  the replacements, and the last of those is [[Error Correcting Code]] read as a hardness
  assumption.

## Core Facts to Know

- **Kerckhoffs's principle**: assume the adversary knows the algorithm. Only the key is secret.
- **Key space is necessary and never sufficient.** A general substitution cipher has $26!$ keys and
  falls to a letter count.
- Attack models climb: ciphertext-only, known-plaintext, chosen-plaintext, chosen-ciphertext.
  Claim security against a named one or you have claimed nothing.
- Monoalphabetic ciphers preserve the frequency distribution; polyalphabetic ones flatten it. A
  [[Transposition Cipher]] preserves it exactly, which is how you recognise one.
- $IC \approx 0.067$ for English, $\approx 0.038$ for uniform. Splitting a Vigenère ciphertext into
  the right number of columns makes each column's $IC$ jump back to 0.067, which recovers the key
  length.
- The alphabet is $\mathbb{Z}_{26}$, so an affine cipher needs $\gcd(a,26)=1$ to be invertible.
  Same theorem as $[a]$ invertible in $\mathbb{Z}_n$ iff $\gcd(a,n)=1$.
- **Confusion** comes from substitution, **diffusion** from permutation. A purely linear cipher of
  any depth collapses to one linear map and is solved by linear algebra.
- A block cipher is a **keyed permutation of the block space**; it must be a bijection or you
  cannot decrypt.
- A [[Stream Cipher]] encrypts by XOR, so encryption and decryption are the same operation. That is
  characteristic 2: $x + x = 0$.
- **Never reuse a keystream.** $c_1 \oplus c_2 = m_1 \oplus m_2$ and the key drops out entirely.
- The one-time pad is unbreakable and unusable: the key is as long as the message.
- An LFSR is a [[Shift Register]] with XOR feedback. Period $2^n - 1$ with a primitive tap
  polynomial, and **broken by $2n$ known keystream bits**, because it is linear.
- A [[Feistel Network]] round is $L_{i+1} = R_i$, $R_{i+1} = L_i \oplus F(R_i, k_i)$. **$F$ is never
  inverted**, so it need not be invertible, and decryption is the same circuit with reversed
  subkeys.
- DES died of a 56-bit key, not a structural flaw. Double DES is not worth doing: meet-in-the-middle
  breaks it at $2^{57}$, trading memory for time.
- [[AES]] is a substitution-permutation network, 128-bit blocks, 10/12/14 rounds for 128/192/256-bit
  keys. Not a Feistel cipher.
- **A [[Byte]] is an element of $GF(2^8)$.** Addition is XOR; multiplication is carry-less multiply
  reduced mod $x^8+x^4+x^3+x+1$. Every non-zero byte has an inverse, which $\mathbb{Z}_{256}$
  cannot offer.
- **The AES S-box is inversion in $GF(2^8)$** followed by an affine map, and it is the cipher's only
  non-linear step. MixColumn is a matrix over the same field.
- **Never use ECB.** Identical plaintext blocks give identical ciphertext blocks, which is
  monoalphabetic substitution one abstraction level up.
- CBC needs an unpredictable IV and encrypts serially. CTR turns the block cipher into a stream
  cipher, parallelises, needs no padding, and dies on nonce reuse.
- **Encryption gives confidentiality only.** Detecting tampering needs a MAC, and the order is
  **encrypt-then-MAC**.
- Public-key operations are roughly $10^3\times$ slower per byte than symmetric ones, so **every
  real system is hybrid**: public-key handshake, symmetric bulk encryption.
- Every public-key scheme rests on an **average-case hardness assumption**, not a theorem. Neither
  factoring nor DLP is known to be NP-complete, and **NP-hardness is the wrong shape** because it is
  worst case.
- **RSA**: $n = pq$, $\phi(n) = (p-1)(q-1)$, $ed \equiv 1 \pmod{\phi(n)}$. Encrypt $m^e$, decrypt
  $c^d$. Correctness is Euler's theorem, which is [[Lagrange's Theorem]].
- $\phi(n)$ **is** the trapdoor, and knowing it is equivalent to knowing the factorisation.
- $d = e^{-1} \bmod \phi(n)$ is computed by the extended [[Euclidean Algorithm]]. **Modular
  inversion and RSA key generation are the same computation.**
- Modular exponentiation is square-and-reduce, $O(\log e)$ multiplications with intermediates never
  exceeding $n^2$. Without it none of this is computable.
- **Textbook RSA is deterministic and therefore broken.** Padding (OAEP for encryption, PSS for
  signatures) is mandatory, not cosmetic.
- **DLP**: given $g^x = h$ in a cyclic group, find $x$. Generic attacks cost $O(\sqrt{n})$;
  **Pohlig-Hellman** reduces it to the largest prime factor of the group order, so use a safe prime
  and a prime-order subgroup.
- **Index calculus is sub-exponential in $\mathbb{Z}_p^*$ and has no analogue on elliptic curves.**
  That single missing algorithm is why 256-bit ECC matches 3072-bit RSA.
- Diffie-Hellman: exchange $g^a$ and $g^b$, both compute $g^{ab}$. **It has no authentication and
  falls to a man in the middle**; signing the exchange is the only fix.
- Ephemeral Diffie-Hellman gives **forward secrecy**: stealing the long-term key later does not
  decrypt recorded sessions.
- A [[Cryptographic Hash Function]] wants pre-image, second pre-image, and collision resistance.
  The generic costs are $2^n$, $2^n$, and **$2^{n/2}$**.
- Collision resistance is cheapest to attack because the attacker picks **both** messages: the
  birthday bound, growing with the number of **pairs**. So SHA-256 gives 128 bits of collision
  resistance.
- **A cryptographic hash is not a hash-table hash.** Collisions are a break rather than an expected
  event, and slowness is a feature. See [[Hashing]].
- Merkle-Damgård leaks by **length extension**, because the digest is the internal state. That is
  why $H(k \| m)$ is not a MAC and why [[HMAC]] nests two hashes. SHA-3's sponge is immune by
  construction.
- MD5 and SHA-1 are broken. SHA-2 and SHA-3 are fine.
- A MAC proves the message came from *someone with the key*, so it gives no non-repudiation. A
  signature does, because only one party holds the private key.
- **You sign $H(m)$, so a hash collision is a signature forgery.**
- **DSA's nonce $k$ must be fresh and secret.** Reuse gives two linear equations and the private key
  falls out; this is how the PS3 signing key was recovered. Ed25519 derives $k$ deterministically.
- The security target for signatures is **existential unforgeability under adaptive chosen-message
  attack**: forging on garbage counts as a break, and the attacker gets a signing oracle.
- The points on an elliptic curve over a finite field form an **abelian group**, with the geometry
  giving the operation. Scalar multiplication $kP$ replaces $g^k$, and ECDLP replaces DLP.
- **Shor breaks RSA, DH, and ECC in polynomial time. Grover only halves symmetric key lengths**, so
  AES-256 survives at 128 bits. Shor's core is the quantum
  [[Discrete Fourier Transform|Fourier transform]].
- "Harvest now, decrypt later" makes the migration urgent for anything that must stay secret for
  decades. NIST standardised ML-KEM and ML-DSA in 2024, both lattice based, and deployments run
  them **hybrid** with the classical scheme.

## Related courses

- [[ABSTRACT ALGEBRA]] (MATH 2101) is the stated prerequisite and it earns it line by line.
  [[Modular Arithmetic]] is $\mathbb{Z}_n$ and modular exponentiation; [[Euclidean Algorithm]]'s
  extended form **is** modular inversion, which is RSA key generation; [[Lagrange's Theorem]] gives
  Fermat and Euler, which is why RSA decryption works; [[Finite Field]] gives $GF(2^8)$, which is
  what the [[AES]] S-box inverts in; [[Cyclic Group]] is the object [[Diffie-Hellman]] and
  [[ElGamal]] run in; [[Group]] and [[Irreducibility]] are what make the curve group and the field
  construction legal. Four notes there name this course by name.
- [[INFORMATION STRUCTURES]] (COMP 2631) owns the homograph. [[Hashing]] and [[Hash Function]] are
  the *other* kind of hash, and [[Cryptographic Hash Function]] states the distinction as a table.
  The birthday argument is shared: it is why a hash table needs collision resolution and why a
  digest must be twice the security level you want. Baby-step giant-step, the standard
  [[Discrete Logarithm Problem]] attack, is a hash-table meet-in-the-middle.
- [[INTRODUCTION TO COMPUTABILITY]] (COMP 2613) supplies the complexity vocabulary and one crucial
  correction to it. [[NP-Complete]] already says NP-complete is not undecidability; this course adds
  that **NP-hardness is not average-case hardness**, and cryptography needs the latter. Neither
  factoring nor DLP is known NP-complete, and that is fine.
- [[COMPUTING MACHINERY 2]] (COMP 2659) is where the [[Stream Cipher]] block lands in hardware. An
  LFSR is a [[Shift Register]] built from [[Flip-Flop]]s with XOR feedback, and
  [[Boolean Algebra]] is $GF(2)$ described from the circuit side.
- [[COMPUTING MACHINERY]] (COMP 2655) holds the bottom rung of the error ladder in
  [[Error Detection]], and [[Integer Representation]] is arithmetic in $\mathbb{Z}_{2^n}$, the same
  modular reduction this course does deliberately.
- [[STATISTICS]] (MATH 2234) is what [[Cryptanalysis]] actually is. Frequency analysis is a
  goodness-of-fit test, the index of coincidence is a collision [[Probability]], and the
  [[Chi-Square Test]] is the standard way to score a candidate key. [[Random Numbers]] is the other
  half: a keystream is a pseudo-random generator, and a weak one has drained real Bitcoin wallets
  through [[Digital Signature|DSA]].
- [[INTRODUCTION TO COMPUTER SCIENCE 2]] (COMP 1633) has the implementations of the number theory:
  [[Prime Number]] with trial division, [[GCD and LCM]] as Euclid in a loop, and
  [[Division Algorithm]] as `/` and `%`. All three of those notes already point here.
- [[FOURIER AND COMPLEX ANALYSIS]] (MATH 4199) meets this course inside Shor's algorithm. The
  [[Discrete Fourier Transform]] is the period-finding step, and the [[Roots of Unity]] that make
  the [[Fast Fourier Transform]] work are the same cyclic structure a discrete logarithm hides in.
- [[LINEAR ALGEBRA]] (MATH 1203) is doing real work in two places: [[AES]]'s MixColumn is a
  [[Matrix]]-vector product over $GF(2^8)$, and lattice-based
  [[Post-Quantum Cryptography]] is a [[Vector Space]] question with integer coefficients.
- [[THE NEW TURING OMNIBUS]] (`Books/`) covers this material as a single chapter, in
  [[Cryptography]]. [[Error Correcting Code]] there is the same finite-field algebra pointed at
  noise instead of an adversary, and McEliece turns it back into a cryptosystem.
- [[WEB DEVELOPMENT FOR CS]] (COMP 3612) is where all of this is deployed, and
  [[HTTPS]] in `Web Interview Prep/` names the three guarantees it buys. Unpacked, an HTTPS
  connection is an ephemeral [[Diffie-Hellman]] exchange, authenticated by a chain of
  [[Digital Signature|signatures]] up to a [[Certificate Authority]], deriving an [[AES]] key that
  encrypts the [[HTTP]] traffic in an authenticated [[Modes of Operation|mode]]. Confidentiality is
  the cipher, integrity is the [[HMAC|MAC]], authentication is the signature: **three different
  primitives for three different guarantees**, and that is the mapping worth carrying out of the
  course.
